about: Hearings and people from official public records. Summaries are written in our own words. Quotes are short and taken word for word from US congressional transcripts and written testimony (US federal records, public domain), checked against the files in data/raw/hearings/. Each entry links to the official source.

hearings.title: House Armed Services hearing on UFOs
hearings.summary: Two weeks after a wave of sightings in Michigan, Air Force Secretary Harold Brown and Project Blue Book's science adviser J. Allen Hynek answered questions from Congress in the first hearing devoted to UFOs.
text: In March 1966 dozens of people around Dexter and Hillsdale, Michigan, reported glowing lights over swampy ground. The Air Force's answer, which the press boiled down to "swamp gas", was mocked across the country, and Michigan congressman Gerald Ford asked for a hearing.

On April 5 the House Armed Services Committee put the question to the Air Force. Secretary Harold Brown read a letter giving the official numbers: 10,147 reports from 1947 to 1965, of which the Air Force said it had identified 9,501. That left 646 listed as unidentified, about 6 percent.

Dr. J. Allen Hynek, the Northwestern University astronomer who had advised Project Blue Book since 1952, used his statement to ask for something new: a panel of civilian scientists to look at the cases that would not go away. Blue Book's project officer, Maj. Hector Quintanilla, sat beside them.
The hearing led straight to the Air Force contract with the University of Colorado, the study run by physicist Edward Condon that would report in 1969.

quotes.q: We can't just write them off. There are too many responsible people who are concerned.
One is led to ask whether there might not indeed be a signal somewhere in the noise.

hearings.outcome: The Air Force set up an outside scientific study, which became the Condon Report.

hearings.title: House Symposium on Unidentified Flying Objects
hearings.body: House Committee on Science and Astronautics
hearings.summary: Six scientists spent a day telling Congress whether UFOs deserved real study, while the Air Force's own study at the University of Colorado was still under way.
text: This was not a hearing on any one sighting. Rep. J. Edward Roush chaired a one-day symposium where scientists from different fields gave their views, and six more sent written papers for the record.

J. Allen Hynek spoke first. Atmospheric physicist James E. McDonald of the University of Arizona said he had interviewed several hundred witnesses in about two years and urged a much bigger scientific effort. Carl Sagan, then at Cornell, talked about the odds of life elsewhere and refused to take either side on what UFOs were. Sociologist Robert L. Hall, engineer James A. Harder and aerospace scientist Robert M. L. Baker Jr. rounded out the panel.
Written papers came from the astronomer and well-known sceptic Donald Menzel, and from Stanton Friedman, R. Leo Sprinkle, Garry Henderson, Roger Shepard and Frank Salisbury.
Six months later the Condon Report concluded that further study was unlikely to add to science, and Project Blue Book closed in December 1969.

quotes.q: I have interviewed several hundred witnesses in selected cases, and I am astonished at what I have found.
The question is very much an open one, and it is certainly too soon to harden attitudes and make any permanent contentions on the subject.

hearings.outcome: No action followed. The Condon Report (1969) recommended against more study and Blue Book closed.

hearings.title: House Intelligence hearing on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena
hearings.body: House Intelligence Subcommittee on Counterterrorism, Counterintelligence and Counterproliferation
hearings.summary: The first open congressional hearing on UFOs in more than 50 years. Two senior Pentagon officials showed Navy footage and admitted some of it had no explanation.
text: Ronald Moultrie, the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, and Scott Bray, the Deputy Director of Naval Intelligence, testified in public before going into a closed session.

Bray said the UAP Task Force database had grown to about 400 reports since the 2021 preliminary report, partly because pilots felt less stigma about reporting. He played two short clips. One showed a reflective sphere flashing past a Navy cockpit. Asked by Rep. Adam Schiff what it was, Bray said he could not say.

He also told the committee the task force had no material from any UAP and nothing that pointed to a non-terrestrial origin. Months later the Pentagon replaced the task force with the office that became AARO.

quotes.q: I do not have an explanation for what this specific object is.

hearings.outcome: Congress created AARO in the 2023 defence budget.

hearings.title: Senate hearing on AARO's mission and budget
hearings.body: Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Emerging Threats and Capabilities
hearings.summary: AARO's first director, Sean Kirkpatrick, gave the new office's first public account to Congress: most reports are ordinary, a few are not, and he would not close cases he could not defend.
text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand chaired the hearing, with Sen. Joni Ernst as ranking member. Dr. Sean Kirkpatrick had run the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office since it opened in July 2022.

He told senators that most reports turned out to be balloons, drones, clutter or natural effects, and that only a very small share looked anomalous. He showed an unresolved video of an orb over the Middle East and explained that many cases simply lacked enough data to solve.
Kirkpatrick also said AARO had found no credible evidence of extraterrestrial activity or of technology beyond known physics. He left the post at the end of 2023.

quotes.q: Only a very small percentage of UAP reports display signatures that could reasonably be described as 'anomalous.'
I will not close a case that I cannot defend the conclusions of.

hearings.outcome: AARO went on to publish annual reports and its historical record review in 2024.

hearings.title: House hearing with David Grusch, David Fravor and Ryan Graves
hearings.body: House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs
hearings.summary: A former intelligence officer said under oath he had been told of a decades-long crash retrieval programme, and two Navy pilots described what they saw. The most-watched UFO hearing ever held.
text: Three men testified. Ryan Graves, a former F/A-18F pilot with the VFA-11 squadron, described unknown objects his squadron began tracking off Virginia Beach in 2014 after a radar upgrade, including one that split two jets on a training flight. David Fravor, retired commander of the VFA-41 squadron, told the story of the 2004 Tic Tac off San Diego.

David Grusch, a former Air Force officer who worked for the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the National Reconnaissance Office, said he had been told of a crash retrieval and reverse engineering programme and denied access to it. He said he could give names and locations only in a closed setting.

The Pentagon denied Grusch's claims, and AARO's 2024 historical review said it found no evidence of such a programme. Members of Congress from both parties kept pushing for disclosure laws all the same.

quotes.q: A dark gray or a black cube inside of a clear sphere.
I was informed in the course of my official duties of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program.
Sir, you are not going to believe this, but that thing is at your CAP point.

hearings.outcome: Led to the UAP Disclosure Act proposals and to AARO's historical record report.

hearings.title: Mexican Congress public hearing on UAP
hearings.summary: The first UFO hearing in a national legislature outside the US. Remembered for two small mummified bodies presented as non-human, a claim scientists widely rejected.

hearings.title: House hearing: UAP, Exposing the Truth
hearings.body: House Oversight subcommittees on Cybersecurity, IT and Government Innovation, and on National Security
hearings.chair: Rep. Nancy Mace and Rep. Glenn Grothman
hearings.summary: A retired admiral, a former Pentagon official, a former NASA official and a journalist asked Congress for more openness about UAP, each from a different angle.
text: Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, a former acting head of NOAA, described a January 2015 Navy exercise off the US East Coast. An email marked as an urgent safety of flight issue went to commanders with the clip now known as Go Fast attached, warning of near-misses. He said the email vanished from his account the next day.

Luis Elizondo, who says he ran the Pentagon's AATIP effort, opened by stating that UAP are real and that the US holds UAP technology. Mike Gold, a former NASA associate administrator who sat on NASA's independent UAP study team, spoke about stigma and the need for open science. Journalist Michael Shellenberger submitted a long document he said came from whistleblowers.

The Pentagon disputes Elizondo's account of his role and his claims about recovered technology. The hearing ended with calls for a single office to handle reports and stronger protection for people who come forward.

quotes.note: the subject line of the 2015 Navy email, as Gallaudet recalls it

quotes.q: Let me be clear: UAP are real.

hearings.outcome: No law passed, but the 2025 House task force picked up the thread.

hearings.title: Senate hearing with AARO director Jon Kosloski
hearings.body: Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Emerging Threats and Capabilities
hearings.summary: AARO's director told senators his office had more than 1,600 reports, that most turn out to be balloons, drones, birds or satellites, and that a few are still very anomalous.
text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand chaired the open session, with Sen. Joni Ernst as ranking member. Gillibrand opened with the drone incursions over Langley Air Force Base and other bases, and asked how AARO would handle cases it had parked in its archive for lack of data.

Dr. Jon Kosloski said AARO now held more than 1,600 UAP reports. He showed charts of what they turn out to be: mostly balloons and drones, with a growing number of satellite flares from big constellations such as Starlink. Most reports come from between 15,000 and 25,000 feet, which he said is mainly because that is where the military's sensors are.

He walked through example cases on slides, including one where an object seemed to fly through a volcanic plume until 3D modelling showed it was 170 metres away. He also said the office had found no verifiable evidence of anything extraterrestrial, and that some objects remain unexplained.

quotes.q: To date, AARO has not discovered any verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology.
AARO does not believe every object is a bird, a balloon, or a UAV. We do have some very anomalous objects.

hearings.outcome: AARO promised a public reporting form and updates on cases it is still studying, not only solved ones.

hearings.title: House task force hearing: Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency
hearings.body: House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets
hearings.summary: Three service veterans described what they saw at Vandenberg, off San Diego and at Langley, a Las Vegas reporter laid out 38 years of paper trail, and a watchdog lawyer explained why whistleblower law matters here.
text: Rep. Anna Paulina Luna chaired, with Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member. Former Air Force security officer Jeffrey Nuccetelli described five incidents at Vandenberg Air Force Base between 2003 and 2005, starting with a large glowing red square seen over two missile defence sites in October 2003.

Senior Chief Alexandro Wiggins, still serving in the Navy, said that in February 2023 the crew of USS Jackson watched a Tic Tac-shaped light rise from the sea off Southern California and join three others before all four left together. He said it was recorded on the ship's sensors.

Dylan Borland, a former Air Force imagery analyst, described a silent triangle about 100 feet long over Langley Air Force Base in the summer of 2012. KLAS-TV reporter George Knapp, covering the subject since 1987, spoke about documents rather than sightings. Joe Spielberger of the Project On Government Oversight argued for stronger whistleblower protection.

quotes.q: We sent information up, but no guidance came down.
Belief has nothing to do with it.

hearings.outcome: Came months before the Pentagon's 2026 PURSUE file releases.

people.name: J. Allen Hynek
text: An astronomer at Ohio State and later Northwestern University, Hynek was hired by the Air Force in 1948 to explain sightings away. He stayed with Project Sign, Grudge and Blue Book for about 20 years and slowly came to think a small core of cases deserved real study.
He testified in 1966 and again in 1968. After Blue Book closed he founded the Center for UFO Studies and gave the world the "close encounters" scale, first, second and third kind.

people.name: Harold Brown
people.role: US Secretary of the Air Force
text: A physicist who ran the Air Force from 1965 to 1969 and later became Secretary of Defense. In 1966 he gave Congress the Blue Book totals: 10,147 reports, 646 still unidentified, and agreed to an outside scientific review.

people.name: Hector Quintanilla
text: The longest-serving head of Project Blue Book, from 1963 until it closed in 1970. He sat with Secretary Brown and Hynek at the 1966 hearing.

people.name: L. Mendel Rivers
text: South Carolina congressman who chaired the 1966 hearing and told the Air Force it could not simply write the sightings off.

people.name: James E. McDonald
text: A respected cloud physicist who became the most outspoken scientist calling for serious UFO study in the late 1960s. He interviewed hundreds of witnesses himself and criticised both Blue Book and the Condon study.
At the 1968 symposium he gave the longest statement of the day.

people.name: Carl Sagan
text: Sagan spoke at the 1968 symposium on the chances of life elsewhere. He said the evidence was not persuasive that UFOs were alien craft, nor that none of them were, and later became one of the best-known sceptics of UFO claims.

people.name: Robert L. Hall
text: Hall spoke at the 1968 symposium on how rumours and mass belief work, and why that alone did not explain the reports he had looked at.

people.name: James A. Harder
text: An engineering professor at Berkeley who spoke about the physics of reported UFO behaviour at the 1968 symposium.

people.name: Robert M. L. Baker Jr.
text: An orbital mechanics specialist who presented his analysis of UFO films and the case for better sensor coverage at the 1968 symposium.

people.name: Ronald Moultrie
people.role: Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security
text: The senior Pentagon intelligence official who testified at the 2022 House hearing and oversaw the setup of AARO.

people.name: Scott Bray
text: Bray ran the public side of the Navy's UAP work in 2021 and 2022. At the 2022 hearing he showed footage, gave the count of about 400 reports, and said plainly when he could not explain something.

people.name: Sean Kirkpatrick
text: A physicist and intelligence official who led AARO from 2022 to the end of 2023. His testimony set the office's tone: most cases are ordinary, some lack data, and none so far point to alien technology.
After leaving he wrote publicly that claims of hidden crash retrieval programmes came from a small circle of people repeating each other.

people.name: Jon Kosloski
text: Dr. Jon Kosloski took over AARO after Sean Kirkpatrick left at the end of 2023.

In November 2024 he gave senators the office's numbers in public: more than 1,600 reports, most of them solved as balloons, drones or satellites, a small share still anomalous, and no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial technology.

people.name: Ryan Graves
text: Graves flew with the VFA-11 squadron off the US East Coast, where crews began tracking unknown objects on radar, infrared and by eye in 2014. He later founded Americans for Safe Aerospace to help pilots report what they see.
He testified to the US Congress in 2023 and also spoke at the Mexican Congress hearing that September.

people.name: David Fravor
text: Fravor led the flight that met the Tic Tac off San Diego in November 2004, working with the USS Nimitz group. He described a white, Tic Tac-shaped object with no wings or rotors moving abruptly over the water, which then turned up at his squadron's planned meeting point about 60 miles away in under a minute.

people.name: David Grusch
text: A former Air Force officer and intelligence civilian who served on the Pentagon's UAP Task Force. He filed a whistleblower complaint in 2022 and in 2023 told Congress under oath that the US runs a hidden crash retrieval programme. He said he was told of it, not that he saw it.
The Pentagon denies the programme exists, and AARO's historical review found no evidence for it.

people.name: Tim Gallaudet
text: An oceanographer who commanded the Navy's meteorology and oceanography command and later served as acting head of NOAA. He testified in 2024 about the 2015 Go Fast email and the near-misses it reported.

people.name: Luis Elizondo
text: Elizondo says he led the Pentagon's AATIP effort before resigning in 2017 in protest at secrecy. The Pentagon has disputed parts of that account. He became the public face of the 2017 New York Times story and told Congress in 2024 that UAP are real and that the US holds UAP technology.

people.name: Mike Gold
text: A space lawyer and former NASA official who sat on NASA's independent UAP study team. At the 2024 hearing he argued that stigma, not secrecy alone, has held back proper science.

people.name: Michael Shellenberger
text: Shellenberger testified in 2024 and submitted a long document on an alleged secret UAP programme that he said came from whistleblowers. Its claims have not been confirmed.

people.name: Jeffrey Nuccetelli
text: Nuccetelli spent 16 years as an Air Force military police officer. In 2025 he described five incidents at Vandenberg Air Force Base from 2003 to 2005, one of which he saw himself, and said reports went up the chain with no answer.

people.name: Alexandro Wiggins
text: A serving Navy operations specialist with about 23 years in uniform. He testified in 2025 about four Tic Tac-shaped lights seen from USS Jackson off Southern California on February 15, 2023.

people.name: Dylan Borland
text: A geospatial intelligence specialist in the Air Force from 2010 to 2013. He told the 2025 task force about a silent triangle he saw at Langley Air Force Base in 2012 and said he has faced reprisals since reporting.

people.name: George Knapp
text: Knapp has reported on UFOs since 1987, including the Bob Lazar story. In 2025 he told Congress he is not a believer or a witness, just a reporter following a paper trail.

people.name: Joe Spielberger
people.role: Senior policy counsel, Project On Government Oversight
text: A watchdog lawyer who testified in 2025 that whistleblower protections matter whatever the subject, and that national security whistleblowers are the least protected.
